title: Deal Velocity, Not Billable Hours: How Crosby Uses AI to Redefine Legal Contracting — publisher's transcript
pub: Sequoia Capital, Training Data podcast, ep. 61 (guests Ryan Daniels and John Sarihan of Crosby; hosts Sonya Huang and Pat Grady)
author: Sequoia Capital

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer

st.t: AI contracting: Deal velocity can undermine negotiation
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition: Crosby delivers legal work through an AI-first law-firm model, prioritises turnaround time over billable hours, and expressly recognises that speed incentives can compromise negotiating interests. It presents lawyer oversight and customer-aligned quality guardrails as necessary controls, while treating minute-scale reviews and broader access gains as aspirations rather than demonstrated quality-adjusted productivity.
qs: If you add up all the time that Crosby has spent looking at a contract, that’s our north star metric.
And the reason that matters so much is because it’s very easy to get misaligned incentives of, like, taking shortcuts, or doing work that’s, like, halfway there.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source supports the proposition that AI may displace junior and paralegal work while leaving experienced lawyers to supervise agents, creating concern about future training opportunities. It also recognises that legal judgment comes from repeated practice and suggests making expertise more explicit, but does not substantially develop the cluster’s proposed programme of simulation, mentorship and independent practice.

kp.k: Delivering legal work enables integrated automation
kp.d: Ryan Daniel describes Crosby as an AI-first law firm focused entirely on contracts, rather than a software supplier. Its strategy is to understand and perform legal work internally, then replace as much as possible with agentic processes. Current scope comprises NDAs, MSAs and DPAs; he characterizes merger agreements as substantially more complex rather than part of the current offering.
qs: So Crosby is an AI-first law firm. We focus entirely on contracts.

And it turns out the best way to do this and to automate it is by building an in-house law firm, understanding how lawyers work and then trying to replace as much of that agentically to get contracts closed faster.
So right now we focus on NDAs, MSAs, DPAs.

kp.k: Partnership economics constrain speculative technology investment
kp.d: Daniel argues that traditional legal services privileged human capital because specialized work could not previously be delegated to technology. He attributes limited innovation partly to partnership financing constraints, and contrasts this with accounting and consulting businesses moving toward corporate structures. Atrium and Clearspire are presented as earlier attempts whose coordination and technology limitations differed from today's opportunity; this is his structural interpretation, not a documented comparative study.
qs: But a law firm partnership, for example, doesn’t allow you to invest in speculative things like building technology because you can’t sell equity, and only law firm partners can take loans that are recourse.
And we’ve seen great innovation in accounting, actually, in management consulting.
huge chunks of the qualitative, thoughtful work that lawyers are doing each day can actually now be delegated to machines.

kp.k: Embedded lawyers create operational feedback beyond benchmarks
kp.d: John Sarihan argues that lawyers working beside engineers provide workflow knowledge, product-use feedback and granular judgments unavailable from benchmarks alone. Crosby reports alternating lawyer and engineer desks and instrumenting contract touchpoints, their duration and turnaround SLAs to prioritize automation that improves customer outcomes rather than simply increasing software releases.
qs: having your domain experts sit side by side with your engineers creates such a unique feedback loop, where it’s more than just evals, it’s actually using the product, experiencing it, doing user research
we literally in our office have desks staggered: lawyer, engineer, lawyer, engineer
here are all the individual touchpoints, here’s how long each touch point took, and here are the highest value touchpoints we can automate today

kp.k: Per-document pricing aligns incentives with efficiency
kp.d: Daniel says Crosby rejected hourly billing from inception and currently bills by document. Pricing requires predicting the work involved, including negotiation rounds, while maintaining quality and alignment with client value. He qualifies the critique of hourly billing by acknowledging its durability and suitability for sophisticated work whose effort is difficult to estimate in advance.
qs: which is no billable hour.
And so what that looks like today is billing by the document.
And it makes a lot of sense for really sophisticated work where it’s hard to ex-ante predict how much work it will be.
being able to predict from time zero how long this piece of work is going to take so that we can price it

kp.k: Deal velocity is the primary customer proposition
kp.d: Daniel identifies deal velocity, rather than AI novelty or low price, as Crosby's central value to rapidly growing clients such as Cursor and Clay. Faster individual reviews and more selective negotiation can both accelerate agreement. He reports median contract review times slightly below one hour and frames reduction to minutes as a goal conditional on appropriate lawyer oversight; the transcript supplies no independent performance validation.
qs: For these companies—and we’ve really crystallized this over several months—it’s deal velocity.
if we just agree to this term and only push back on these three, we’re going to save one turn, so this will be a whole week faster.
right now we do a contract review and median times are at a little under an hour.
Can we get that to minutes while still having—making sure that the right terms get in front of the right lawyers at the right times?

kp.k: Speed metrics require client-specific quality guardrails
kp.d: Sarihan defines total turnaround time, TTAT, operationally as the sum of Crosby's time reviewing a contract across all negotiation rounds, not simply the whole elapsed negotiation period. Crosby also seeks to reduce human review time, HuRT. In response to the host's concern that speed could encourage concessions, he says a dedicated lawyer-engineer team assesses quality, customer risk profiles and negotiation interests alongside these efficiency measures.
qs: If you add up all the time that Crosby has spent looking at a contract, that’s our north star metric.
We have people on the team, both lawyers and engineers, only focused on how do we make sure quality is consistently meeting our customers’ needs.
is this aligned with our customer’s risk profile?
We also called this other metric, it’s called HuRT, which stands for Human—hu—review time—RT.

kp.k: Lawyer oversight and liability underpin buyer trust
kp.d: Daniel invokes legal services as a credence good whose quality buyers, including sophisticated CEOs, cannot judge without expertise. Crosby retains lawyers to check substantive work, carries malpractice insurance and accepts liability. He predicts that lawyers will remain involved in many types of legal work, with escalation design determining when their approval is necessary. This describes supervised service delivery, not current autonomous reliance.
qs: A layperson—or even not a layperson, a sophisticated CEO—often doesn’t know by definition how good their legal work is.
because lawyers provide almost an insurance to make sure that an expert said something looks good, they’ll always be in a loop for a lot of types of legal work.
right now we have malpractice insurance; we take liability for all the work we do.

kp.k: Context and individualized alignment address inconsistent legal judgments
kp.d: Sarihan proposes first equipping lawyers with contextual workflow tools, then aligning model behavior with particular lawyers and customers. He argues that individual consistency offers a useful target when reasonable lawyers disagree, and recommends per-customer evaluations, prompts and fine-tuning. His claims that models reach 90 percent easily but struggle to reach 99 or 99.99 express a general reliability argument, not measured Crosby accuracy results.
qs: today, it starts with how can you context engineer for a human lawyer, right?
Really what you want to do in some of these specific scenarios is align it to a specific person, right?
I think per customer fine tuning and evals are a really high ROI way, especially if you have a large ACV
they get to 90 percent, and getting them to 99 or 99.99 is actually extremely difficult.

kp.k: Negotiation data could quantify tacit risk judgments
kp.d: Daniel and Sarihan suggest translating lawyers' market intuitions and risk heuristics into probabilistic guidance on contract terms, such as governing law. They present this as an emerging opportunity rather than an established validated capability. Both emphasize missing contract data: Daniel identifies EDGAR as an overused dataset poorly matched to smaller companies, while Sarihan says available models are not specifically tuned for contracts.
qs: taking the vibes and heuristics inside of a lawyer’s head and converting that into an actual probabilistic quantitative number
how likely should you be to accept Delaware or California or New York governing law when you’re in the specific negotiation?
The best data set is EDGAR.
that data has just been so overutilized, and doesn’t apply to these smaller companies.

kp.k: AI assists explanations while lawyers control substantive edits
kp.d: Daniel reports that nuanced contractual wording is harder for AI than expected, so experienced lawyers currently drive substantive editing. He identifies summarization, explanatory comments and delivery of company-specific product information as stronger applications. He says Crosby learned in May that thoughtful explanations help counterparties accept changes and reduce negotiation turns. Sarihan reports early experimentation with reinforcement fine-tuning for comment generation, without providing comparative results.
qs: the subtleties of the ways you change language within a contract are something that AI seems to struggle with a bit more than we’d imagined.
the difference between the term “commercially reasonable” and “reasonable” are actually substantively different things to a lawyer, but look very similar in an embedding space.
you have lawyers sort of driving and really kind of intervening for the quality on actual edits to a contract.
reinforcement fine tuning was something we experimented with early on for comment generation

kp.k: Routing automation precedes proposed associate-role substitution
kp.d: Sarihan says Crosby has already built a paralegal agent that routes incoming work to human lawyers. Extending automation to tasks associated with junior associates, senior associates and junior partners is described as the next step, not completed replacement. Task-specific tools, context and customer-specific agents are central to that proposed progression.
qs: Today we’ve basically built a paralegal agent, which is, like, in charge of routing all the work that comes in from our customers
routes it to a human lawyer and makes sure the work is assigned effectively.
The next step is like, how do you think about a junior associate, a senior associate, and a junior partner at a law firm, and think about actually replacing these roles in that way

kp.k: Lawyer formation shifts toward explicit teaching and process design
kp.d: Daniel argues that repetition-based apprenticeship has not required lawyers to become skilled at explaining their tacit expertise, whereas directing AI makes that skill valuable. Crosby encourages lawyers to write prompts, map processes and reduce review time instead of rewarding billed hours. His examples are internal anecdotes, including a lawyer's extensive process map. He advises law students to question professional dogma while respecting legal scholarship and learning to use AI.
qs: You don’t actually spend that much time getting really good at teaching because you just do it through reps and reps and reps and reps.
explaining things is something that I think is going to be a very prized skill
Get them writing prompts.
we give a lot of public praise for being sort of meta aware of the work you’re doing and trying to measure it out.
And so don’t be arrogant, but question everything.

kp.k: Autonomous legal help is forecast for unmet individual needs
kp.d: Daniel predicts complete automation of some individual legal assistance because the alternative is often no assistance, distinguishing new service provision from displacement of existing lawyers. He asserts that about 11,000 US firms represent eight percent of firms and about 75 percent of revenue, with the other 92 percent focused on individuals; no supporting study is identified. He speculates that ChatGPT can already help negotiate leases and hopes greatly expanded lawyer throughput will widen access, while describing corporate legal jobs as relatively safe.
qs: there’s about 11,000 law firms, which account for eight percent of all law firms in the US, that account for about 75 percent of revenue.
I think this work will be automated entirely because the alternative is nothing.
it’s not that we’re taking a lawyer’s job and automating it, it’s just nobody’s doing it today.
I think that the corporate law firms are here to stay for quite a while, and those jobs are quite safe.
rather than looking at two contracts an hour, they can look at 500

kp.k: Agent negotiations remain a future collaborative vision
kp.d: Daniel envisages agents representing each party's preferences, simulating negotiation and presenting an auditable sequence for human consideration. Sarihan emphasizes partitioning confidential data and restricting inter-agent communication. These are aspirations rather than reported deployments. Daniel also maintains that human interaction and creative persuasion retain an essential role in reaching agreement, illustrated by an offshore contracting anecdote.
qs: being able to capture each party’s preferences with their own sets of agents, and have them simulate the negotiation
be able to show an auditable record
these are fundamentally collaborative negotiations; these are not adversarial.
partitioning the data, making sure, like, this agent doesn’t have access to the other agent’s data
there’s an essential role for those counterparties to have in interfacing with each other to have what we call meeting of the minds

kp.k: Senior oversight may expand while junior opportunities contract
kp.d: Asked about the industry in 10 years, Sarihan expresses concern about junior associates and paralegals and imagines a senior associate managing many agents. His hypothetical personal-injury practice automates intake and demand-letter work while concentrating the human role on court appearances and oversight. This is a forecast of changing role composition, not evidence of observed employment losses.
qs: I get a little worried about the junior associates and the paralegals and the opportunity for them.
I can imagine it just looks like a senior associate managing an army of agents
The main job of the person is to show up in court, and everything else is handled by an agentic system.

kp.k: In-house expansion motivates specialized AI-first service providers
kp.d: Daniel reports that in-house legal teams grew 200 percent during 2007–2017 versus 30 percent for law firms, then cites growth from about 320,000 to 440,000 during 2014–2024 without identifying a study or clearly specifying the latter count's unit. He attributes in-house innovation to greater organizational freedom to combine lawyers, paralegals and legal operations. He hopes specialized AI-first providers will increasingly deliver functions currently housed within businesses that do not specialize in legal services.
qs: In the 10-year period from 2007 to 2017, in-house legal teams grew 200 percent and law firms grew 30 percent.
And then again from 2014 until 2024, they went from about 320,000 to 440,000.
They can have not just lawyers, they can have paralegals, they can have legal operations
you’ll see more and more specialized companies that are AI first

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Daniel and Sarihan describe AI-first contracting as a service that accelerates negotiations, changes pricing and lawyer workflows, and may eventually automate underserved work and substantial parts of existing legal roles.
pts.d: Ryan Daniel presents Crosby as an AI-first law firm delivering contract work rather than selling software. He argues that combining lawyers and engineers allows substantive work to be delegated to machines and supports faster innovation than traditional partnership structures. John Sarihan says delivering the service creates operational feedback beyond evaluations and benchmarks. Daniel identifies deal velocity—not primarily lower prices—as customers’ central benefit: faster reviews and more selective, better-explained negotiation positions can reduce negotiation rounds. Crosby bills by document, with predicting workload and negotiation rounds enabling pricing. Both speakers envision converting lawyers’ risk heuristics into quantitative guidance. Sarihan reports an existing routing agent and envisages agents performing associate and junior-partner specialty tasks. Daniel nevertheless expects lawyers to remain involved in much legal work for quality assurance and liability. He predicts growing value for lawyers who can explain expertise and write prompts. For underserved individual legal needs, Daniel predicts complete automation as net-new provision rather than displacement of work currently being done. He anticipates corporate firms persisting and more specialized AI-first service providers emerging. Sarihan’s ten-year scenario is more concerned about junior opportunities: experienced lawyers may manage agents that handle most non-court work. Daniel also envisages agents representing each party’s preferences, simulating negotiations, and providing an auditable proposed agreement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists mainly of founders’ operational experience, self-reported performance and experiments, customer examples, and uncited market statistics; longer-term outcomes are explicitly visions or conjectures.
pts.d: Daniel reports median contract-review times slightly below an hour, identifies Cursor, Clay and Unify as customers, and describes a May observation that thoughtful AI-generated explanations reduce negotiation rounds. Sarihan describes instrumentation of turnaround times, human touchpoints and human review time, alongside a quality team and guardrail metrics. His north-star metric aggregates Crosby’s handling time across negotiation turns; it should not be treated as a reported measurement of complete elapsed deal duration including counterparty delays. The transcript provides no sample size, comparison group or published performance results. The existing routing agent, lawyer-engineer collaboration, lawyer-written prompts and process mapping are experiential examples. Sarihan reports reinforcement-fine-tuning experiments, while his 90 percent versus 99 or 99.99 percent discussion is a general characterization of the difficulty of achieving reliability, not a measured Crosby accuracy result. Daniel reports difficulty distinguishing legally consequential wording and describes lawyer intervention and malpractice coverage. For market predictions, Daniel cites roughly 11,000 firms representing eight percent of US firms and about 75 percent of revenue, and historical in-house staffing growth figures, without identifying sources. The 2007–2017 comparison is 200 percent in-house growth versus 30 percent firm growth; he separately mentions a rise from about 320,000 to 440,000 over 2014–2024 without clearly specifying that series’ population. These historical figures support his market narrative, not a demonstrated causal effect of AI. Complete automation, 500 contracts per hour, and agent-to-agent negotiation are aspirations or scenarios rather than established outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Present capabilities are confined to selected contract workflows with lawyers supervising; fuller automation is conditional and largely undated, with broader industry scenarios framed over five to ten years.
pts.d: At the September 2025 interview, Daniel says Crosby focuses on NDAs, MSAs and DPAs; merger agreements are discussed as much more complex, not as a demonstrated current service. The routing agent and sub-hour median reviews are current claims; reducing reviews to minutes is a goal. Sarihan conditions expansion on repeatability, automatable workflows, good tools and task-specific context. He advocates alignment to individual lawyers and per-customer prompting, fine tuning and evaluations, especially for high-value customer contracts; these are proposed routes to reliability rather than a claim that near-perfect accuracy has been attained. Daniel conditions speed on getting the right terms to the right lawyers, maintaining quality and assuming liability. Sarihan adds customer-risk and negotiation-interest guardrails to prevent speed metrics encouraging concessions or shortcuts. Daniel explicitly allows continued hourly billing for sophisticated unpredictable work and expects lawyers to remain in the loop for many work types. His full-automation prediction concerns unmet individual needs where the alternative is no assistance, while his corporate-job reassurance is qualified as 'for quite a while.' His optimistic professional outlook spans the next five to ten years; Sarihan’s agent-managed staffing scenario and Daniel’s specialized-provider outlook answer a ten-year question. Agent-to-agent negotiation is an undated aspiration and Sarihan conditions it on data separation and controlled communications.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The speakers distinguish faster enterprise contracting, changing professional roles, and access to legal assistance for underserved individuals.
pts.d: Fast-growing B2B technology companies, their salespeople and in-house counsel are the immediate buyers and beneficiaries: faster reviews and fewer rounds are intended to accelerate revenue-generating deals while respecting business risk. Crosby is a provider delivering legal work, not merely a legal-tech vendor or a client’s internal legal department. Its lawyers, many with BigLaw experience, currently drive reviews and verify edits while working with engineers to improve workflows. Daniel sees explanation, prompting and process improvement becoming prized professional skills, including for law students. Sarihan sees senior lawyers gaining capacity through agents but worries about junior associates and paralegals; his personal-injury example allocates intake and drafting to agents, with the person primarily appearing in court. The suggested increase from two to 500 contracts per hour is Daniel’s hypothetical expansion of lawyer capacity, not a reported staffing ratio or measured productivity result. Underserved individuals needing help with leases, child support and similar matters are a separate access-to-justice population: Daniel predicts new assistance where none is currently available. He does not equate those unmet needs with enterprise cost savings.
